title: Fit a day of sensor readings into the gateway's memory

blocks.text: The building gateway keeps the last day of readings from every sensor in memory: one reading every 500 ms, a time in epoch milliseconds and a `double` value, 172,800 readings per sensor per day. The plan is 40,000 sensors on one gateway. The prototype stored each sensor's day in about 36 bytes per reading, which doesn't fit, and its dashboard query, "when was this sensor above the limit?", slowed the gateway down with garbage collections every few seconds.

`capacity()` and `size()` are done. Finish the `TODO`s in `src/main/java/practice/ReadingLog.java`: the storage and the constructor, `append(...)`, `timeAt(...)`, `valueAt(...)` and `timesAbove(...)`.

When you're done, a full day of readings allocates at most 17 bytes per reading, and one query allocates at most 8 bytes per reading in the log plus 8 bytes per time it returns. About fifteen lines in total.
The tests read the thread's allocation counter (`com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes`) around the calls they measure.

cases.says: every reading's time and value read back as appended, in arrival order
a query returns the times of the readings strictly above the limit, in arrival order
a day of 172,800 readings allocates at most 17 bytes per reading
a query allocates at most 8 bytes per reading in the log plus 8 per time it returns

origin.section: An Object Costs a Header Plus Its Fields, Rounded Up to 8 Bytes; a Reference Costs 4 Bytes Below 32 GB

concepts: An object costs a 12-byte header plus its fields, rounded up to 8 bytes; a Long is 24 bytes, so a list of Longs costs about 28 bytes per number against 8 in a long[].
